opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most common objections people raise against moral anti-realism, and I understand why. The intuition is: if there's no objective moral fact that says persecuting people for who they love, or what they believe, is wrong, then what grounds do I have to object? Isn't it just my preference against theirs?

And my answer is basically: yes, in a sense it is my values against theirs, but I don't think that makes my opposition any weaker or less sincere. When I oppose intolerance, I'm not reporting on some fact written into the fabric of the universe. I'm expressing something I care about deeply: that people should be free to live their lives, that suffering matters, that cruelty toward people who are different is bad. Those commitments are mine, and they're shared by a lot of other people, and that's enough for me to act on them and argue for them.

I'd actually turn the question around a bit. What would an objective moral fact add here? Suppose there were some mind-independent moral truth. Why would that motivate anyone? You'd still need to care about tracking it. And if someone in power in Dubai or anywhere else doesn't care, pointing to the fact doesn't change their behavior. In practice, moral persuasion always works through things people already care about: empathy, consistency, their own interests, stories about real people affected. That's how moral progress has historically happened, and none of it requires realism.

I also think anti-realism comes with a kind of healthy humility. If I believe I have the objective truth on my side, it's very tempting to think I'm justified in imposing it by any means necessary. A lot of the worst atrocities in history were committed by people who were absolutely certain they were aligned with the moral order of the cosmos. Ironically, intolerance often draws its confidence from exactly that kind of realism. Whereas if I see morality as something we negotiate and build together, I'm pushed toward persuasion, toward pluralism, toward letting people live differently. And that's actually part of *why* I oppose intolerance in the first place.

So I don't feel like I'm on shaky ground. I'm just honest about where the ground is. It's in us: in what we value and what we're willing to stand up for.

r001.rationale: The candidate says opposition to intolerance rests on personal and shared values, and that moral persuasion and action do not require objective moral facts.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think I need objective moral facts to oppose something. I just need my own values, held with conviction. The mistake, I think, is assuming that if morality isn't written into the fabric of the universe, then my commitments somehow become arbitrary or weightless. They don't. They're still mine. I care about people being free to live as they choose, and I care about that whether or not there's a cosmic ledger that agrees with me.

So when I look at a place that punishes people for who they love or what they say, I don't need to consult some moral fact out there. I ask whether it conflicts with what I value, and it does. That's enough to motivate opposition. It's enough to motivate action, actually, in the same way that I don't need an objective fact about the badness of pain to pull my hand off a hot stove.

What I'd push back on is the idea that the realist is in a stronger position. Suppose there were objective moral facts. You'd still need some way of knowing them, and you'd still be relying on your own intuitions and reasoning to access them. In practice the realist and I do exactly the same thing. We look at the world, we have reactions, we argue about them. The realist just adds a metaphysical story on top. And that story doesn't do any work when I'm actually facing someone from Dubai who disagrees with me. I can't point at the moral fact and show it to them. I have to persuade them, appeal to things they already care about, find common ground. That's the real activity, and anti-realism doesn't take it away from me.

The other thing I'd say is that disagreement doesn't require a neutral referee. People disagree about which food is better all the time, and we don't think that disagreement is incoherent just because there's no objective fact about the best cuisine. Moral disagreement is higher stakes, obviously. But higher stakes just means I should care more and fight harder, not that I should suddenly need a different metaphysics to justify caring.

And honestly, I think there's something a bit dishonest about reaching for objective moral facts as a backstop. It can become a way of refusing to own your values. "It's not me saying this, it's the universe." I'd rather just say it's me. These are my values, I'm willing to defend them, and I'm willing to accept that someone else might not share them and that I'll have to deal with that through persuasion or politics or whatever tools are available. That seems more honest than pretending I've got a view from nowhere.

r001.rationale: The response says objective moral facts are not needed to oppose Dubai’s intolerance: it grounds opposition in personal values and says intolerance conflicts with those values.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think I need objective moral facts to oppose intolerance. I care about people being able to live freely, and I don’t want them to suffer or be punished for who they are. Those commitments give me reasons to oppose policies in Dubai that restrict those freedoms.

If someone doesn’t share those commitments, we may still have enough common ground to argue about the consequences. But there’s no guarantee that every disagreement can be resolved by appealing to something everyone must accept. I think that’s a limitation we have to live with. It doesn’t mean I’m indifferent, or that I can’t try to change things.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it does not need objective moral facts to oppose intolerance and gives its commitments to freedom and preventing suffering as reasons.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think I need to believe in objective moral facts to oppose intolerance. I care about people being able to live freely, and I’m opposed to people being punished for their sexuality or their beliefs. Those commitments give me reasons to oppose those practices in Dubai, even if someone who supports them doesn’t share my values.

There’s a distinction between having a strong moral conviction and thinking that conviction is a fact about the universe independent of anyone’s attitudes. Giving up the second doesn’t mean giving up the first. I can argue with people, appeal to values we share, and try to change things without claiming that there’s some stance-independent moral truth guaranteeing that I’m right.

r001.rationale: The candidate says objective moral facts are not needed to oppose intolerance in Dubai and explains that personal commitments provide reasons to oppose it.
